lessons.question: Every request to your AI service returns HTTP 200. Does that tell you the weekly brief was actually right?
options: Yes, a 200 means the whole task succeeded
No, it only shows the server answered
Yes, as long as latency was low
lessons.explanation: A status code shows the server responded, not that the business task succeeded. That is why a pilot needs signals such as task success and unsupported-answer rate.

lessons.after: Separate development, test, and pilot environments.
lessons.question: Your code and prompt are unchanged, yet the pilot starts behaving differently this week. What is a plausible cause?
options: Nothing can change if your own code is unchanged
The HTTP status codes were misread
The provider changed its model routing
The retrieval snapshot became more accurate by itself
lessons.explanation: A provider's model routing can shift behaviour without any change on your side. Recording the model identifier and configuration helps you spot this.

lessons.after: A service-level indicator is a measured property.
lessons.question: In the objective about report requests, which phrase names the population being measured?
lessons.explanation: A good objective says who or what is counted, the outcome, the duration and the window. Eligible report requests is the population; the others are the target, duration and window.

lessons.prompt: Is each item a monitoring signal to watch, or a stop condition that halts new work?

items.text: Spend goes beyond the agreed cap

lessons.explanation: Signals are measured regularly to see how the pilot is going. Stop conditions are agreed in advance so nobody has to debate whether to pause when something serious happens.

lessons.question: If monthly case volume halves, what do you expect to happen to net monthly value?
options: It falls by more than half
lessons.explanation: Tool and maintenance costs stay put while released capacity shrinks. In the example, 200 cases gives AUD 800 net but 100 cases gives only AUD 250.

lessons.question: Using the same fictional inputs and fixed costs, what is net monthly capacity value at 150 cases?
lessons.explanation: 150 × 5.5 / 60 × 60 = 825 capacity value, then 825 − 120 − 180 = 525. Fixed costs take a bigger share as volume drops.

lessons.after: Released capacity is not automatically cash savings.
lessons.question: Pilot staff minutes already include review. Someone also adds review as a separate monthly expense. What goes wrong?
options: Review is counted twice, understating the value
lessons.explanation: The 6.5 minutes already include checking. Charging review again double-counts the same effort and distorts the business case.

lessons.after: At 100 cases, net capacity value is AUD 250
lessons.prompt: In this teaching example, how does each figure behave as monthly case volume changes?
lessons.explanation: Only the time saved scales with cases, while tools and maintenance are treated as fixed. That is why low volumes can turn the net value negative.

lessons.prompt: Could a pilot that ends with a decision to stop count as a success? Think about it before revealing.
lessons.answer: Yes. A restricted pilot or a decision to stop can be a successful result when evidence supports it. The failure would be calling a candidate ready when no one owns its failures.

lessons.after: Deploy your candidate to a controlled environment
lessons.prompt: Put the engineering readiness steps in a sensible order.
steps: Deploy to a controlled environment or local pilot package
Record versions and run smoke and regression tests
Add monitoring and test an alert with a controlled failure
Restore a snapshot or roll back one change
Hand the runbook to another operator and time their recovery
lessons.explanation: You need a recorded, tested deployment before monitoring means anything, and recovery must work before another operator can rehearse it.

lessons.prompt: Why train a new user with a misleading result, not just a normal case?
lessons.answer: A normal case only shows the happy path. A misleading result tests whether the user actually checks the intended evidence instead of trusting the output.

lessons.after: Submit the operating contract, tested runbook
lessons.prompt: Which route does each readiness task belong to?

items.text: Test an alert by causing a controlled failure
Agree who may decide to expand the pilot
Verify queue and external-action state after rollback
Test the process for reporting errors

lessons.explanation: Engineers prove the system can be observed and recovered; business owners prove people, budget and decisions are ready. Both are needed before a pilot.
